n: This is the turning point of the whole story. That very night the king can’t sleep, so he has the royal records read to him. A sleepless night seems like chance, but the book invites us to see God’s quiet hand.

f.w: the book of records of the chronicles

n: Of all the pages, the reader happens upon the account of Mordecai exposing the assassination plot years earlier.
The king asks how Mordecai was rewarded. The answer: nothing was done. In Persia, failing to reward loyalty was considered shameful for a king.

f.w: There is nothing done for him
f.g: Persian kings were known for publicly rewarding their benefactors.

n: At that very moment, Haman arrives early in the morning to ask permission to hang Mordecai. The timing is perfect — for Mordecai.

f.g: The outer courtyard, where people waited to be summoned.

n: The servants tell the king Haman is waiting, and the king calls him in.
The king asks Haman how to honor a man the king delights in. Haman, full of pride, assumes the king means him.

f.w: To whom would the king delight to do honour more than to myself?

n: Haman begins his answer eagerly, repeating the king’s phrase.
He asks for the king’s own robe, the king’s own horse, and a royal crest — honors that would make him look almost like the king himself.

f.w: the crown royal which is set upon his head
f.g: Probably the royal crest on the horse’s head; Persian art shows horses with such ornaments.

n: He wants a top noble to dress the man and lead him through the city, announcing his honor. Haman is designing his own dream parade.
The king’s reply is a stunning reversal: do all this for Mordecai the Jew — the very man Haman came to kill. Leave nothing out.

f.g: Don’t leave out a single detail.

n: Haman must dress his enemy in royal robes, lead him through the streets, and shout his praises. His plan for honor becomes his public humiliation.
Mordecai quietly returns to his post at the gate, unchanged. Haman rushes home in grief, covering his head in shame.

f.g: A sign of mourning or humiliation (2 Samuel 15:30).

n: Haman tells his wife and advisers, who now warn him: if Mordecai is a Jew, you have begun to fall and will not win against him. Even his own household senses a higher power at work.

f.w: thou shalt not prevail against him

n: Before Haman can recover, the king’s servants arrive to hurry him to Esther’s banquet. Events are now moving faster than he can control.
